(CNN) -- China's Olympic adventure may be over, but new age chanteuse Sa Dingding is one global export that in many ways echoes the Beijing Olympic fantasy of "One World. One Dream." Sa Dingding's music should find a home on the iPods of millions of chill-out world music fans. Born to a Mongolian mother and Han Chinese father, she sings in Mandarin, Tibetan, Sanskrit, and the rare dialect of Lagu, while fusing chill-out beats and floaty instrumentation played on zither, horse head fiddle and bamboo flute. Already hugely popular in China, she has been finding similar success farther afield: Her first album sold 2 million copies in Southeast Asia, and she has appeared on MTV. Earlier this year she won a BBC Radio 3 World Music Award as well as performing at the Royal Albert Hall in London. Her linguistic skills and musicianship were honed from a young age. Born in Inner Mongolia in 1983, she spent three years until the age of 6 with her grandmother, living a nomadic life in northern China, where her imagination and creativity were allowed to roam free. "We actually lived in a small city between grassland and the big city. In spring time, we move to the grassland. And in winter time, we moved back to the city,"she told CNN's Talk Asia. "The whole memory of my childhood is in one word: Play. I just played everywhere on the grassland. And there a lot of interesting things happened which affected the ... life of mine." Later she became a student of Buddhism and yoga as well as becoming a multi-instrumentalist, releasing her first album at the age of 18. Melding different musical cultures and ethnic influences, notably Tibetan, has also caused a certain amount of discussion, especially on her own position toward the status of Tibet within China. "From a musician's point of view, Tibetan culture and its music cannot be seen as an isolated subject... lots and lots of other ethnicities have added their colors on the Tibetan culture. So I see the Tibetan culture nowadays as an integral part of the greater Chinese culture," she said. Aiming to avoid controversy, organizers of the Glastonbury festival dropped her from this year's lineup. "I don't quite understand the reason behind [it]. To me, art and music really belong to the whole world and they shouldn't be limited by boundaries. So I really hope that I could join Glastonbury next year," she said. Until then further explorations in language and music beckon, and there have been recent collaborations with house music DJ Paul Oakenfold and French chill-out duo Deep Forest in Europe. "It's very amazing because when I had to return to China, they drove me to the airport and told me: 'Life is full of miracles. When you first arrived here, these three songs didn't exist. But now you're leaving, and we have three wonderful new songs.'"

While China's time hosting the Olympics has come to a close, singer Sa Dingding continues to carry forward the spirit of unity captured in the Games' motto, "One World. One Dream," through her distinctive artistry on the world stage.

Her sound is poised to captivate countless listeners who favor ambient, genre-blending world music. The daughter of a Han Chinese father and Mongolian mother, she performs in an unusual mix of languages—Mandarin, Tibetan, Sanskrit, and the obscure Lagu dialect—while blending relaxed electronic rhythms with traditional instruments like the zither, morin khuur (horse head fiddle), and bamboo flute.

Her domestic fame in China has translated into international acclaim as well. Her debut record moved 2 million units across Southeast Asia, earning her airtime on MTV. This year alone brought her a BBC Radio 3 World Music Award and a performance slot at London's prestigious Royal Albert Hall.

Sa Dingding's gift for languages and music took shape early in life. Following her 1983 birth in Inner Mongolia, she spent her early years—until age six—living with her grandmother in a nomadic community across northern China, an environment that nurtured her imagination without constraint.

"We actually lived in a small city between grassland and the big city. In spring time, we move to the grassland. As she matured, she immersed herself in Buddhist teachings and yoga practice, mastering multiple instruments along the way and releasing her debut album at just 18.

Her practice of weaving together diverse musical traditions—particularly Tibetan elements—has sparked debate, particularly regarding her views on Tibet's political relationship with China.

"From a musician's point of view, Tibetan culture and its music cannot be seen as an isolated subject... lots and lots of other ethnicities have added their colors on the Tibetan culture. So I see the Tibetan culture nowadays as an integral part of the greater Chinese culture," she stated.

Sa Dingding shows no signs of slowing her creative exploration across languages and genres. She's recently partnered with DJ Paul Oakenfold and the French ambient group Deep Forest on European projects.

Despite her artistic acclaim, Sa Dingding's career has not been without controversy. This tension reflects larger, unresolved questions about cultural ownership, political context, and artistic freedom that continue to follow Sa Dingding throughout her career.

Whether viewed as a bridge-builder or a controversial figure, she remains a compelling example of how music can simultaneously unite and provoke in an interconnected world.

# Between Two Worlds: How Sa Dingding Is Redefining Global Sound

In a Beijing studio filled with guzheng, morin khuur, and an array of synthesizers, Sa Dingding is doing what she's always done best—refusing to choose sides. The artist, who first captured international attention with her 2007 album *Alive*, has spent over a decade building bridges between ancient Chinese and Mongolian musical traditions and the pulsing landscapes of Western electronic production.

"I never thought of it as fusion," she says, settling into a chair still humming with the residual energy of a late-night recording session. "For me, these sounds were never separate. The throat singing, the electronic beat—they come from the same place. They come from breath, from rhythm, from something ancient in the body."

That philosophy has attracted some unexpected collaborators. When legendary DJ and producer Paul Oakenfold reached out to work together, Sa Dingding admits she was initially cautious.

"Paul understands space in a way that surprised me," she explains. "Trance music and Mongolian long-song actually share this quality—they're both about suspension, about taking the listener somewhere and making them forget time. When we worked together, he kept telling me, 'Don't change your melody for me. Let me build around you.' That trust changed how I thought about collaboration."

Oakenfold, for his part, has spoken about the experience in similarly reverent terms, noting in press materials how Sa Dingding's vocal work offered "a texture I couldn't manufacture with any synthesizer—something with centuries behind it."

The relationship with Deep Forest, the pioneering French world-electronic duo, came from a different angle entirely. Where Oakenfold brought dancefloor sensibility, Deep Forest's Éric Mouquet approached with the atmospheric, sample-based ethos that made the group famous in the 1990s.

"Deep Forest taught me something about patience," Sa Dingding reflects. "Éric would sit with a single phrase I sang—maybe five seconds—for hours. He wasn't trying to complete it or resolve it. He wanted to live inside that sound. It reminded me why I started singing in endangered languages in the first place. Some things shouldn't be resolved. They should just be witnessed."

Mouquet has echoed this sentiment in interviews, describing Sa Dingding's voice as possessing "an otherworldly quality that doesn't need our production to justify its existence—we're just framing something already complete."

### A Different Kind of Crossover

What makes Sa Dingding's collaborations notable isn't simply the pairing of East and West—that framing, she argues, is itself outdated. "Journalists always want this story: traditional artist meets modern producer, magic happens. But Paul and Éric aren't rescuing my music or translating it. We're just three people who love sound trying to make something none of us could make alone."

She's quick to note that these partnerships haven't diluted her commitment to preservation. Sa Dingding continues to research and perform in Sanskrit, Tibetan, and several Mongolian dialects, some spoken by fewer than a thousand people. "The electronic elements bring new listeners to these languages," she says. "A teenager in Berlin hearing a trance remix might then look up where the vocal sample comes from. That curiosity is worth something."

As she prepares new material that she describes as "even more unafraid" than her earlier work, Sa Dingding remains characteristically unbothered by genre classifications. "People ask what category my music belongs to," she laughs. "I tell them: put it wherever you want. I'm not trying to fit into world music or electronic music. I'm trying to make music that feels like being alive—complicated, layered, a little bit ancient and a little bit new, all at once."
